source_text: Τὰ δὲ περὶ τῆς εἰδωλολατρείας ὡς ἴδια τῶν ἀπὸ τοῦ λόγου ἐκτιθέμενος καὶ ὑποκατασκευάζει λέγων αὐτοὺς διὰ τοῦτο μὴ νομίζειν αὐτοὺς χειροποιήτους θεοὺς, ἐπεὶ μὴ εὔλογόν ἐστι τὰ ὑπὸ φαυλοτάτων δημιουργῶν καὶ μοχθηρῶν τὸ ἦθος εἰργασμένα εἶναι θεοὺς, πολλάκις καὶ ὑπὸ ἀδίκων ἀνθρώπων κατασκευασθέντα. ἐν τοῖς ἑξῆς οὖν θέλων αὐτὸ κοινοποιῆσαι ὡς οὐ πρῶτον ὑπὸ τούτου εὑρεθὲν ἐκτίθεται Ἡρακλείτου λέξιν τὴν λέγουσαν· „ὅμοια, ὡς εἴ τις τοῖς δόμοις λεσχηνεύοιτο, ποιεῖν τοὺς προσιόντας ὡς θεοῖς τοῖς ἀψύχοις.“ οὐκοῦν καὶ περὶ τούτου λεκτέον ὅτι ὁμοίως τῷ ἄλλῳ ἠθικῷ τόπῳ ἐγκατεσπάρησαν τοῖς ἀνθρώποις ἔννοιαι, ἀφ᾿ ὧν καὶ ὁ Ἡράκλειτος καὶ εἴ τις ἄλλος Ἑλλήνων ἢ βαρβάρων τοῦτ᾿ ἐνενόησε κατασκευάσαι. ἐκτίθεται γὰρ καὶ Πέρσας τοῦτο φρονοῦντας, παρατιθέμενος Ἡρόδοτον ἱστοροῦντα αὐτό. προσθήσομεν δὲ καὶ ἡμεῖς ὅτι καὶ Ζήνων ὁ Κιτιεὺς ἐν τῇ Πολιτείᾳ φησίν· „ἱερά τε οἰκοδομεῖν οὐδὲν δεήσει· ἱερὸν γὰρ οὐδὲν χρὴ νομίζειν οὐδὲ πολλοῦ ἄξιον καὶ ἅγιον, οἰκοδόμων τε ἔργον καὶ βαναύσων.“ σαφὲς οὖν ὅτι καὶ περὶ τούτου τοῦ δόγματος γέγραπται „ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις“ τῶν ἀνθρώπων γράμμασι θεοῦ τὸ πρακτέον.
pass_a_gloss: The things concerning idolatry being set forth as proper to those from the word and he subconstructs saying they on account of this do not think them to be handmade gods, since it is not reasonable that the things made by the most wicked and evil-natured creators are gods, often even constructed by unjust men. Therefore, wanting to make this common in the following, he sets forth the saying of Heraclitus which says: 'Similarly, as if someone were to make a shelter for the houses, to do to the approaching ones as to the lifeless gods.' Therefore, it is to be spoken concerning this that similarly to the other ethical topic, notions have been sown among men, from which also Heraclitus and if any other Greek or barbarian has thought to construct this. For he sets forth also the Persians thinking this, placing Herodotus as narrating it. We will add also that Zeno the Citian says in the Republic: 'There will be no need to build temples; for nothing ought to be considered sacred or worthy of much and holy, the work of builders and craftsmen.' It is clear therefore that also concerning this doctrine it has been written 'in the hearts' of men with the letters of God what is to be done.

pass_b_english: He takes up the question of idolatry as something that belongs especially to those who draw their teaching from the Word, and he reinforces his case by arguing that people should not regard handmade objects as gods, since it is not reasonable that things fashioned by the most worthless craftsmen—men of evil character, often unjust—should be considered divine. Wishing to show that this insight is not original to Christian teaching, he next cites a saying of Heraclitus: 'It is like someone who builds a shelter for houses and treats the lifeless idols inside as if they were gods to be approached.' The point is that, just as with other ethical principles, God has sown this understanding in human hearts; from that seed Heraclitus, and any other Greek or barbarian who grasped it, drew the same conclusion. He also adduces the Persians as holding this view, quoting Herodotus as his witness. We may add Zeno of Citium, who writes in his Republic: 'There will be no need to build temples; for nothing ought to be considered sacred or worthy of great honor and holiness, since temples are merely the work of builders and craftsmen.' It is therefore clear that this doctrine, too, has been written ‘in the hearts’ of men with the letters of God, showing what is to be done (Romans 2:15).

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Greek text. Pass A provides a literal gloss, while Pass B provides a fluent translation. Pass B correctly identifies and adds the implied scripture citation (Romans 2:15) for 'written in the hearts', which is required by the instructions for added identifications. The Heraclitus quote and the Zeno quote are rendered faithfully in both versions.
